newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thais ready to accept austerity package - advisor.
newsitem.headline: Thais ready to accept austerity package - advisor.

text.p: The Thai government is ready to accept an IMF package that includes a credit line to bolster foreign reserves, further budget cuts, and a rise in its value added tax, a senior government advisor said on Tuesday.

"I think the Thai government is very ready to adopt austere policies, to adopt a new package to deal with the financial institutions, and I think the government is very ready to have a further budget cut," government advisor Surakiart Sathirathai told Reuters Financial Television.
Surakiart, a former finance minister, has not been directly involved in government negotiations with IMF officials but is a close financial advisor of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchayudh.

Any credit line secured should go directly to foreign reserves which have been depleted by the central bank's defence of the currency in the run up to the baht's de facto devaluation on July 2, Surakiart said.
"My personal view is that (a) certain portion would be for the foreign reserves, whether there are additional loans for additional purposes remains to be seen," Surakiart added.

"As far as the foreign reserves (are) concerned we don't know the exact figure, but it is our belief that if the IMF programme is in place, confidence will be restored but I personally do not expect a big size of loan," he said.
Thailand has previously suggested it requires between $10-20 billion dollars to help stabilise the ailing economy.
Stability, rather than renewed growth, was the focus of the package and the government was prepared to accept budget cuts to achieve its goals, Surakiart said.
"We are not very concerned about economic growth at the moment, we are concerned more with the stability issue," he said.
Budget cuts could be made on non-essential economic and social items like defence, he said.

"That would be one area, not only military cuts but any imports which are not necessary would be subject to cuts, but I think the details of the budget cuts would have to be discussed further," he said.
Value added tax (VAT) could rise to 10 percent from seven percent but negotiations were continuing as to whether VAT would be increased gradually, he said.

"It has been a case of our studies that value added tax will have to increase up to 10 percent. The question is whether it will be increased immediately or it will increase gradually, step by step," Surakiart said.
Income and corporate tax cuts were also likely, he said.
"Secondly we have studied whether corporate tax can be reduced, together with personal income tax," he said.
As part of plans to revamp the fragile financial system, regulatory bodies were also likely to be overhauled, he said.
"I think for the rest of the financial institutions there has to be a revision, especially of the central bank's supervision," he said.
"There have been discussions on the deposit insurance scheme that should be established in order to protect depositors," Surakiart said.

"As far as the real estate is concerned I think measures to deal with non-performing loans, not with bad assets, would have to be put in place so the financial institutions can be free of non-performing loans and continue to consolidate or to merge," he said.
